body.text: China appears to be interfering in campaigning for Taipei’s 28 November mayoral election, running a disinformation effort against a candidate from the independence-minded Democratic Progressive Party.

Beijing also seems to have taken steps to support its preferred candidate, the current mayor, Chiang Wan-an, who’s from the main Taiwanese party that favours closer links with the mainland, the Kuomintang (KMT).

The challenger, Puma Shen, last year expressed concern that the city was maintaining an official exchange with China through the Taipei–Shanghai Twin City Forum. Under Chiang’s policy, Taipei hosts the forum every other year. It’s the only remaining official channel of dialogue across the Taiwan Strait, because China cut all the others in 2016. Shen now says that if he wins the election he’ll attend the forum next year, as long as China sets no political preconditions and the forum delivers practical benefits to Taipei. These demands have been too much for Beijing, which has rejected his offer. Its Taiwan Affairs Office said Shen was ‘in no position to talk about cross-strait exchanges and cooperation’.
Shen also champions civilian preparedness and is the former CEO of Doublethink Lab, an organisation that resists digital authoritarianism, including by tracking Beijing’s influence around the world.

Overt pressure on Shen was seen most recently on 13 October, when two Hong Kong state-run newspapers accused his father of using a second company to evade Chinese sanctions that had been imposed on another of his businesses. The next day, the Taiwan Affairs Office repeated the allegation and sanctioned the firm. Taiwan’s Mainland Affairs Council called this election interference.

This pressure has also extended to Taiwanese television host Kevin Tsai after he attended Shen’s campaign launch on 4 October. Several Chinese businesses distanced themselves from him. Chinese electric-vehicle manufacturer Leapmotor removed promotional content featuring Tsai, while all content on his Weibo account disappeared overnight. On 6 October, Jun Zhengping, a media account affiliated with the Chinese armed forces, indirectly criticised Tsai’s attendance without naming him.

This tactic is familiar: in October, Chinese sponsors dropped French football star Kylian Mbappe, and Chinese broadcasters suspended La Liga coverage, following his remarks about a ‘Chinese dictator’ – implied to be Mao Zedong – which prompted Mbappe to publicly apologise.

Hidden pressure on Shen is cruder. In June, a Facebook page circulated manipulated images purporting to show Shen using drugs, a tactic previously used by China in the Philippines and by Russia in France. Watchout, an independent Taiwanese media outlet, found the Facebook page listed at least one administrator in China. Its investigation also found that the page had previously paid to promote posts about Mazu, a sea goddess widely worshipped in Taiwan, with advertising records identifying funders based in China. Such lifestyle content draws in followers who would skip a political page. Who made the fabricated images remains unclear.

A second deepfake, an audio clip exploiting the issue of US arms sales, purported to capture Shen admitting to taking a bribe. Taiwan’s Ministry of Justice Investigation Bureau confirmed the audio was synthetic and identified a man in Taoyuan, Taiwan, as having posted it on Threads. Legal action was swiftly taken. Taiwanese outlet SETN noted that the synthetic voice impersonating Shen in the clip referred to Taiwan as ‘the island’, a term more commonly used in China. Accounts behind the clip have yet to be publicly linked to Beijing.

Shen’s online campaign platform was also subject to cyberattack from foreign IP addresses. Hackers breached a campaign server and flooded a supporter sign-up platform with more than 70,000 fake registrations in an hour. The campaign said it had contained both attacks and restored normal operations.

Chiang, meanwhile, was the subject of a wave of favourable Facebook posts. In September, at least six Facebook pages, several run by Hong Kong-based administrators, published sympathetic stories portraying Chiang as a caring father amid allegations that his son had received preferential treatment in a student exchange program. Two pages misspelt his wife’s name in the same way, suggesting a common information campaign source. So far, no link to Chiang’s campaign has been verified, and he has publicly opposed foreign influence. In October, 22 accounts on Threads, several linked to Hong Kong telephone numbers, posted graphics crediting the KMT with securing access to Chinese markets and urging voters to act on 28 November.

Beijing denies interfering in Taiwan’s affairs. Yet Taiwan’s National Security Bureau says China has been using fake accounts and AI-generated material to influence public opinion. By tracking suspicious online accounts, it recorded about 2.5 million disputed posts in the first nine months of 2026, 48 percent more than a year earlier, on subjects including energy, food safety and defence. How many voters were swayed through information operations is unknown.

While China’s hand in some of the election interference is still unproven, whoever is behind the pressure on Shen understands the weight that Taiwanese society places on filial piety, the duty to respect and care for one’s parents and elders. An accusation against his father casts the son as the cause of his family’s trouble, and the charge is hard to rebut without drawing more attention to it.
